I. BACKGROUND
1. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the applicants and Mr.
Tushar Mehta, the learned Solicitor General appearing for the Union
of India.
2. In our previous order dated 14.08.2026, we had expressed concerns
over certain serious lapses on the part of various social media
intermediaries and platforms, particularly in complying with the
directions that were issued in our judgment dated 23.09.2024 in Just
Rights for Children Alliance & Anr. v. S. Harish & Ors. reported in
2024 INSC 716.
3. In Just Rights (supra) we had taken note of an alarming increase in
child sexual exploitation and abuse material ("CSEAM") that were
being circulated on social media platforms.
4. At that time, we had flagged how indirect links to such harmful
material were being promoted and shared through social media
algorithms to bypass the rigours of the special penal provisions

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 4 of 136
designed for the protection of children within the cyberspace, namely
Section(s) 15 and 67B of the POCSO Act1 and the IT Act2
, respectively.
5. In our judgment, more particularly at paragraph 109, we had this to
say: -
"109. During the course of hearing, our attention was also
drawn to a recent news article that reported how on social
media, links to view child pornography were being circulated
and sold for anywhere between Rs. 40 to Rs. 5,000. The news
report indicates, how social media platforms are rife with child
sexual abuse, and gave certain insight about the modus
operandi of the distribution of such material on these platforms.
It explained how the sellers and distributors of child
pornographic material rather than sharing any downloads to
such material, would ingeniously only share links to such
material instead in lieu of money, so as to circumvent the penal
provisions of the POCSO and IT Act, which criminalized only
the storage of such material. By indefinitely forwarding links,
they completely bypass the requirement of first storing such
material onto any device, and similarly those who view such
material also only use the links, without ever downloading
such material onto their device."
(Emphasis supplied)
6. We had further taken note of the disquieting failure on part of the
social media platforms in reporting such harmful activities to the
Special Juvenile Police Unit, as required by the law.
1 The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short, the "POCSO Act").
2 The Information Technology Act, 2000 (for short, the "IT Act").

7. In this regard we had this to say: -
"256. It has been brought to the notice of this Court that social
media intermediaries do not report such cases of child abuse
and exploitation to the local authorities specified under
POCSO and rather only comply with the requirements
stipulated in the MOU. In view of the salutary object and the
mandatory character of the provisions of Sections 19 and 20 of
the POCSO read with Rule 11 of the POCSO Rules, we are of
the considered view, that an intermediary cannot claim
exemption from the liability under Section 79 of the IT Act for
any third-party information, data, or communication link
made available or hosted by it, unless due diligence is
conducted by it and compliance is made of these provisions of
the POCSO. We are also of the view that such due diligence
includes not only removal of child pornographic content but
also making an immediate report of such content to the
concerned police units in the manner specified under the
POCSO Act and the Rules thereunder.
xxx xxx xxx
258. In view of the overriding effect of the POCSO Act and the
rules thereunder, merely because an intermediary is in
compliance of the requirements specified under Section 79 of
the IT Act, will not absolve it of any liability under the
POCSO, unless it duly complies with the requirements and
procedure set out under it, particularly Section 20 of POCSO
Act and Rule 11 of the POCSO Rules. It is a settled position
of law, that when a statute describes or requires a thing to be
done in a particular manner; it should be done in that manner
or not at all. Thus, social media intermediaries in addition to
reporting the commission or the likely apprehension of
commission of any offence under POCSO to the National
Centre for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) is also
obligated to report the same to authorities specified under
Section 19 of POCSO i.e., the Special Juvenile Police Unit
(SJPU) or the local police."
(Emphasis supplied)

8. We had clarified in no uncertain terms that such failures would strip
the social media platforms of the "Safe Harbour" protection provided
by Section 79 of the IT Act.
9. We had hoped that the above inter-alia directions would bring a
quietus to the disturbing widespread circulation of CSEAM on the
internet.
10. We had hoped that we would not have to, once again, be confronted
with the same sad state of affairs.
11. Despite more than two years having gone by since our judgment, it
appears that there has been no progress worth the name. If anything,
the recent news reports instead reveal an even more unsettling reality
when it comes to the safety and wellbeing of our children.
12. We are deeply saddened to note that the news reports placed before
us by the applicants flagging alleged incidents of paid promotions of
CSEAM on social media platforms through redirect links and websites
is only one rare instance of such harmful activities being discovered
and brought to light.

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 7 of 136
13. There are millions of more such incidents freely available on social
media platforms that may never come to the knowledge of the proper
authorities, if no collective action is taken today by all stakeholders.
14. There comes a time when we must ask ourselves, how many more
victims of such harmful content must continue to suffer, before our
conscience is stirred into making collective effort in the right direction.
15. We are afraid that we cannot afford to wait any longer for an answer.
Due to the lack of any earnest initiative shown on the part of either the
regulatory authorities or the social media intermediaries for all these
years, we are left with no choice but to take matters in our own hands.
16. We cannot emphasize this enough, that there can be no space for non-consensual sexually exploitative and abusive material on the internet,
particularly on platforms that are readily accessible to the most
impressionable and vulnerable of our society.
17. Thus, with the assistance from the Union of India through the Ministry
of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Law
and Justice, respectively, we propose to take the strictest of actions by

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 8 of 136
putting in place a workable framework for a safer future of our
children.
18. In this regard, there are certain aspects which we must point out that
merit a considered response, and we would like to hear the Union of
India on the same.
II. FRAMEWORK FOR THE DETECTION AND REMOVAL OF
CSEAM.
A. Advanced Mechanisms for the Detection and Removal of CSEAM
i. Some Problems in the Existing Mechanism.
19. As far as we understand, the current mechanism for the detection and
removal of CSEAM relies heavily on individual instances of content
being reported and subsequently removed. These reports originate
either at the behest of the authorities or the users themselves.
20. Although, various social media intermediaries have deployed their
own safeguards for a seamless continued detection and removal of
such content, yet what is missing is any form of synergy insofar as
detection and removal is concerned, across the internet.

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 9 of 136
21. When one social media platform detects and removes CSEAM, that
detection does not automatically result in the same content being
flagged and removed from all other social media platforms.
22. It is only when such content is also found by the other platforms,
through their own mechanisms and safeguards that, the same comes
to be removed.
23. This isolated mechanism of detection delays the removal of CSEAM
across different platforms, delays which enable the continued
circulation of such content to the various corners of the internet.
24. Even if some social media platforms are coordinating their efforts for
the simultaneous removal of CSEAM once so detected by either of one
of them, such arrangements are only informal, dependent entirely on
which platforms choose to undertake such initiative and for how long.
ii. Matching and Listing of Hash & URL of CSEAM.
25. From what we have been able to understand, the practice that is
globally in vogue for the seamless detection and removal of CSEAM
is a process termed as "Hash and URL Data Matching & Listing".

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 10 of 136
26. The process works on a simple principle. Every component of a
CSEAM content, be it the video frame or image or multiples of both,
carries a unique digital data print identifier in alphanumeric form,
which is known as the "Hash" identifier of that material. The hash
identifier of any particular content remains unique to it, irrespective
of where it is uploaded or by whom.
27. When any content is identified as CSEAM, specialised software is
used to extract and generate the hash identifier and the same is added
to a consolidated database known as a "Hash List".
28. This Hash List can then be used to crosscheck all other content,
whether on the very same platform or on another. Where a match is
found against a particular hash identifier, the algorithm automatically
flags and removes that content without the need to rely on the
conventional means of detection.
29. However, the above mechanism is not without limitations. Expert
insights indicate that a new modus operandi has emerged for
circumventing the hash list detection process. This is usually done by
manipulating the video frame or imagery of the content, or a

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 11 of 136
combination of both, either by way of resizing it or reformatting it, so
as to avoid detection.
30. It is for this reason that "Perceptual Hashing", an improved process of
recent vintage assumes significance. Shorn of the details, this process,
from what we understand, combines the original technique of
extracting the hash identifier with an additional step of generating the
audio-visual characteristics of the content. Characteristics such as
colour-coding, object composition, audio cues, etc., are also used to
generate the hash identifier for a content detected as CSEAM, which
remains unique dehors any manipulation.
31. One another technological measure of similar significance that has
caught our attention is URL Listing, which targets indirect links to
CSEAM and other harmful content that are merely shared or
exchanged on social media platforms without uploading or storing the
same on the platform.
32. The news report that has been placed before us by the applicant herein
reveals the prevalence of this very practice. It highlighted the
circulation and promotion of CSEAM through links which would then

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 12 of 136
redirect users to other websites and platforms where such materials
were offered for monetary considerations.
33. "URL Listing" thus, assumes significance. Unlike Hash Listing that
generates a unique identifier for the CSEAM content, URL Listing
proceeds by generating an identifier for the external location where
the CSEAM content is hosted. It extracts all possible unique web-addresses where the CSEAM has been confirmed to have been
uploaded, and then uses that data to block any future attempts to
access it.
34. Various jurisdictions across the world have, in some form or manner,
called for the deployment of one, or a combination of the aforesaid
measures, with a view to ensure the effective detection and removal
of CSEAM.

iii. The Position in India.
35. From what we can discern, no such provision exists in India, requiring
social media intermediaries to employ tools for Hash or URL Listing,
at least to the same extent as found in other jurisdictions.

37. These rules which came to be inserted by the Information Technology
Amendment Rules, 2026, although a step in the right direction, yet,
fall short as they do not speak of the specific tools and measures a
social media intermediary must adopt.

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 17 of 136
38. Rule 3(1) sub-clause (b), inter-alia, requires that intermediaries make
reasonable efforts to ensure that their users do not host, upload or
disseminate any CSEAM and other non-consensual sexually
exploitative and abuse material, including those generated artificially,
and to further remove such material under sub-clause (c).
39. Whereas Rule 4(4), inter-alia, requires a "significant social media
intermediary" to also deploy "appropriate technical measures" for the
detection and removal of CSEAM, including materials which are
identical in content to any material that was previously flagged and
deleted "on the computer resource of such intermediary".
40. We would be remiss not to point out that the expression "on the
computer resource of such intermediary" used in Rule 4 sub-rule (4)
admits of certain ambiguities which need to be addressed.
41. In our considered view, the said expression narrowly confines the
extent to which the technical measures must be deployed for the
detection and removal of CSEAM.
42. The emphasis placed by Rule 4(4) on only that CSEAM content, which
has been either detected or previously removed from the

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 18 of 136
intermediary's own computer resource, leaves unresolved two
possible scenarios. First, the possibility of simultaneous flagging and
removal of CSEAM content that was already removed on some other
platform. Secondly, CSEAM content that is hosted on an external
source and merely circulated on a particular platform via indirect
links.
43. To state plainly, under this rule, even if a particular CSEAM was
previously detected and removed by one intermediary, there is no
corresponding obligation cast upon other intermediaries to
automatically look for and remove the same, at least not until, such
material happens to also be detected by them in due course of time.
44. This, in our view, confines the entire obligation of detection and
removal of CSEAM exclusively to material that has been uploaded,
circulated and detected on one intermediary's own resources.
45. We, prima facie, find this to be a matter of some concern, particularly
when there are reported instances of CSEAM being indirectly
circulated, and a less than ideal rate at which such material is currently
being detected and removed. It is needless to reiterate that every

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 19 of 136
moment of delay in removing such harmful content only serves to add
to the certain likelihood of further circulation to other platforms.
46. Even otherwise, the cumulative effect of the above rules is that social
media intermediaries are only required to "make reasonable efforts" and
"deploy appropriate technical measures" for the proactive detection and
removal of CSEAM and other non-consensual sexually exploitative
and abusive material from their platforms.
47. We are conscious of the fact that, at the current pace of advancement
in technology, it is impractical to statutorily prescribe any particular
set of tools and measures for a thriving, safe, and secure cyberspace.
That being said, we see no reason why widely used tools and
measures of proven mettle cannot be stipulated in the form of
periodically revisable guidelines to ensure their uniform and proper
adoption by one and all.
48. We do not, for a moment, doubt that certain social media
intermediaries may already have employed one or more of the
aforementioned tools and measures, or even a combination of all of
them. However, the efficacy of such tools depends not only on their

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 20 of 136
deployment by some, but on their proper and uniform adoption by
all, and that is precisely what specific guidelines in this regard can
ensure.
49. All that we are trying to say is that while a rigid statutory prescription
may not be the appropriate course, yet the same does not, however,
mean that no guidelines should be put in place.
50. We would, therefore, like to hear from the Union of India on the tools
and technological measures that have been put in place by
intermediaries for the detection and removal of CSEAM from their
platforms, including the use of perceptual hash-matching and URL
listing. This is because, in the absence of such information, it would be
difficult for us to assess whether the obligation to "make reasonable
efforts" is, in practice, being discharged in any meaningful manner. We
would further like to hear on the feasibility of a industry-wide use and
deployment of such tools, if not already in use. Lastly, we would like
the Union of India to come up with some comprehensive guidelines
on the tools and technological measures that every intermediary
would be expected to deploy for the detection and removal of CSEAM.

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 21 of 136
B. Comprehensive National Database for the Detection and Removal
of CSEAM.
i. Need for a National Database for Hash & URL Lists of CSEAM.
51. We must, however, point out that the deployment of these tools
cannot be the end of the matter. Unless the hashes and URLs of
CSEAM identified by one intermediary are made accessible to all
others, the very process of simultaneous flagging and removal of such
material across platforms would remain illusory.
52. It is in this context that a national "Hash and URL List Database"
assumes significance. As the name suggests, it is a common repository
or pool of the hash identifiers and URL lists of all material which has
been flagged and confirmed to be CSEAM across all platforms. The
database is continuously updated in real time, and made accessible to
all intermediaries and law enforcement agencies, to enable a seamless
process of detection and removal of CSEAM on a rolling basis.
53. The significance of such a database may best be appreciated by
contrasting it with the current state of affairs. At present, each
intermediary, at best, maintains its own list of known CSEAM,
compiled from what it has encountered on its own platform. The

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 22 of 136
result is a multitude of fragmented lists, each incomplete in itself. The
multiplicity in efforts in the detection and removal of CSEAM that we
seek to avoid cannot take place without such a database.
54. In other words, intermediaries would be in a position to crosscheck
the content on their own platforms against the entire database, and
not merely against what they themselves have encountered in the
past. It is of note that such a database would not contain the harmful
material itself, but only the hash identifiers and URLs by which it may
be recognised.
55. There are outstanding examples of such databases that have played a
pivotal role in reducing the circulation of CSEAM. Various
jurisdictions have entrusted the maintenance of such databases to
designated bodies and organisations that verify each entry before its
inclusion and ensure that the database remains current.

ii. Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre's Sahyog Portal.
56. In this regard, we are given to understand that some progress has
taken place in the right direction. The Union of India has already
developed and put in place a dedicated platform known as the
"Sahyog Portal" to inter-alia streamline and automate the process of
reporting and removal of unlawful content including CSEAM.
57. The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the authority
designated to manage and maintain the portal, has been onboarding
social media intermediaries onto the same, with a view to coordinate
the reporting and removal of CSEAM with the police machinery.
58. We acknowledge that the Sahyog Portal is, no doubt, a step in the right
direction. It is also not lost on us that the portal, by virtue of having

M.A. Nos. 2553-2554 of 2026 Page 24 of 136
already onboarded a considerable number of intermediaries, may well
be the natural foundation upon which a Hash & URL List Database
could be built.
59. That being said, we are mindful of the fact that, the portal, in its
current form, functions only as a common platform to route individual
reports and takedown notices.
60. Our expectations from the portal, however, are much more than what
it is, as of now, capable of doing, and we are hopeful that the Union of
India shares the same vision.
61. We say so because there is a discernible difference between a common
portal that routes individual reports and takedown notices, and one
which pools together the hash identifiers and URLs of all material
confirmed to be CSEAM. The former acts only upon each instance of
